analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "Thank you, gentlemen. The case is submitted. We'll hear arguments next in Consolidated Freightways Corporation against Castle. Mr. Letter, I think you may proceed whenever you're ready. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the Court. There is only one issue which is properly before this Court, and that is the issue of whether or not the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals, in denying attorney's fees under 1988, should have given reasons for its denial. Now, the facts and procedural posture of this case are this. In 1978, Consolidated Freightways brought suit against a number of officials of the state of Iowa, alleging that Iowa's statute and the enforcement of it, which banned 65-foot twin trailers in Iowa, was unconstitutional. The complaint alleged that the actions of the Iowa officials in enforcing that statute were a violation of 42 U.S.C. 1983, but no damages were requested. The complaint did, however, request attorney's fees under 42 U.S.C. 1988. The District Court bifurcated the trial and took the case in chief, putting aside the question of attorney's fees. The District Court found for Consolidated Freightways on the case in chief. The result was appealed to the Eighth Circuit. The Eighth Circuit affirmed. In return, it was brought before this Court, and this Court affirmed also. But you're asking for your attorney's fees in the Eighth Circuit. That is correct. At the conclusion of the appeal in the Eighth Circuit, pursuant to the federal rules of appellate procedure, the clerk of the Eighth Circuit sent a letter directing Consolidated Freightways to file a bill of cost, itemizing therein all costs which they desired to have awarded to them, and warning of waiver if they did not provide all costs. 42 U.S.C. 1988 provides for the award of attorney's fees as cost. To avoid waiver, we filed a bill of cost with the Eighth Circuit that laid out as a separate item attorney's fees under 1988, and we filed with the bill of cost a letter to the Eighth Circuit informing them that the case below had been bifurcated and suggesting that remand to the District Court would certainly serve judicial economy. There was no briefing of the issue of attorney's fees. The Iowa officials filed in response, as is provided for in the rule, a simple statement that they were in opposition, citing no law or in no way constituting a brief. The Eighth Circuit chose not to remand to the District Court nor to request briefs. Instead, it denied attorney's fees, and the substance of their decision is simply one line stating that the motion for attorney's fees is denied. And you say they do not have the discretion to do that? We say that they do not have the discretion to deny attorney's fees without stating the reason for the denial. That's correct. Immediately after the denial, consolidated freightways filed a motion to vacate, requesting either an opportunity to brief the issue or the alternative that the Eighth Circuit vacate its order denying attorney's fees and remand the case to the District Court. Very short summary briefs supporting that motion were filed, but no extensive briefs were filed on the issue of attorney's fees. The Eighth Circuit chose not to vacate its order, denied the motion to vacate. On how many different grounds do you suppose they might have arrested their denial? Your Honor, I guess I don't really know a number. There are three that perhaps seem most likely to me in our brief. We went through an itemized ten. That's a number. That's three. Well, you know, I don't pretend to understand what process. Which one do you think they might have arrested the denial? I think they might have arrested it on the 11th Amendment. Although I think there's law to the opposite in that case. I think they may have arrested it on the argument that 1983 does not particularly cover this situation. I think they may have, in fact, intended in an oblique way to simply send the matter, have the District Court decided initially. And rather than remand... They could have arrested it on any ground that, well, 1988 applies. But as a matter of discretion, we're not going to allow it. Yes, they could have. They could have arrested it on the ground that 1988 applies, but that there were special circumstances in this case that would have prevented it on all the attorney's fees. What was the argument made by the other side in support of the judgment law? I mean, before that court. No argument was made prior to the Eighth Circuit's decision. To the Eighth Circuit at all? No argument was made to the Eighth Circuit at all. Not even briefed? No briefs. The appendix contains the sum and substance. It was a bill of cost, simply itemizing the cost, and a simple statement from Iowa that they were opposed to the allowance of cost. Not saying on what grounds? Not saying on what grounds. There were briefs filed in the Eighth Circuit on the motion to vacate after the Eighth Circuit had already rendered its decision, but there were no briefs filed before the initial decision. And what was the position taken by Iowa on the motion to vacate? Iowa opposed the motion to vacate. On what grounds? On the grounds that 1983 did not apply, and if I recall correctly, on the grounds that... I'm not sure whether they raised the Eleventh Amendment grounds in their brief or not. Did you meet those grounds of objection at all? No. In briefing before the A-C? No. We filed a simple brief supporting the motion to vacate. They filed a brief opposing the motion to vacate, and the Eighth Circuit decided on those two briefs. Well, what I'm trying to get at, what issues did you... On what grounds did you oppose the motion? Did I oppose the motion? I supported it. I'm sorry. We supported it on the grounds that 42 U.S.C. 1988 was applicable, and that no special circumstances existed here. And did you address the 1983 question? We did very summarily, yes. I should make it clear the brief was intended as a brief to support the motion to vacate. Yeah. The motion to vacate requested that the Eighth Circuit, if it desired to decide this issue itself, set up a briefing schedule, permit us to file briefs and affidavits on it. It was not a brief on the issue of whether or not attorney's fees should be awarded. It did cover that issue to the extent of trying to point out to the Eighth Circuit this is a real issue. Well, did the motion request the Eighth Circuit to state the grounds of its denial? Yes, it did. But you must have taken the position that 1983 covered this action. Yes, we did. And that under 1988, the Court of Appeals or the District Court did not possess sufficient discretion to deny your motion for your bill of costs, even though it was covered by your substantive action was covered by 1983. That's correct, Your Honor. Now, we certainly took the position consistently throughout that 1983 applied and that attorney's fees were due us under 42 U.S.C. 1988. The problem or the difficulty... Was your action originally brought in the District Court as a 1983 action? Yes, Your Honor. The complaint as one of the causes of action alleged 1983 and specifically asked for attorney's fees. Do you think under the statute the problem would have been satisfied if the Court simply recited in the exercise of our discretion fees are denied? Or do they have to say A, B, C, D? No. What guided their discretion? I should make clear. I don't think the courts necessarily have to write erudite opinions on each matter that comes before them. All that was necessary here could have been disposed of in one or two sentences. What about the one sentence I just gave you? In the exercise of our discretion, fees are denied. That would have been a closer question, but, yes, I think that would have been adequate. It would have at least provided the parties the idea that what the problem was here was a factual problem, that it was the court exercising its discretion and not making a legal decision that 1983 doesn't apply. The reason why I think some statement of reasoning is required by the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals is perhaps well illustrated by this case. The common practice in most circuit court of appeals for attorney's fees on the appeal is to have that decided by the district court. It's the practice that this court originally encouraged in antitrust cases, Perkins v. Standard Oil, and has been followed fairly consistently by all of the circuits, though I think all of the circuits recognize that they have the power to decide attorney's fees themselves. The Eighth Circuit has not been consistent with the other circuits. It frequently decides attorney's fees itself, setting both the amount of the fees and making the initial decision as to whether or not a fee should be granted. That makes this court the initial court of review. There is no other court to which an appeal can be taken. Well, then does that not demonstrate that they acknowledge that it's a discretionary matter? The practice you've just described, doesn't that suggest that they acknowledge that they had the legal authority under 1988, but it's a matter of discretion, they were not going to give the fees? That's right. That is difficult to square with the statute. The statute provides for an award of fees under this court's interpretation and other courts' interpretations. But you just told me that if they'd recited in the exercise of discretion, the court hereby denies allowance of fees. If the court exercised discretion, then under the interpretation of the statute, they would have found special circumstances. And I think a statement that they exercised discretion logically means that they found special circumstances, which are the instances in which the statute permits attorney's fees not to be awarded, and that would have been enough of a guidance to both this court and to us as attorneys so that we could have at least determined what the issue was on appeal. But aren't you saying in effect that you're willing to lose this case, but you just want the Eighth Circuit to write a couple more sentences? Well, the difficulty is, I don't know that I'd say that I'm willing to lose this case, but what the issue here is, as I see it, is we need to know why it was denied so that we can determine is this an issue that should be appealed? Is this an issue where the Eighth Circuit was wrong? Perhaps the Eighth Circuit's right. And on reflection and reviewing the opinion, we may conclude that, yes, we lost and we lost fairly. The difficulty with this court standing as the only court of appeal, the initial court of review, this court has to pick and choose what cases it's going to hear. And for it to pick and choose what cases it's going to hear, it has to look at petitions for certiorari. We can't determine. What specifically can you point to me to which says that a court has to give reasons? Almost uniformly, every circuit court in reviewing district court decisions on attorney's fees has laid down as an absolute rule that the district court. What rule is it that requires this court here involved, the Eighth Circuit, to do it? This court has previously, in a closely analogous case, North Cross v. Memphis Board of Education, reversed the Sixth Circuit and remanded to it on the grounds that the Sixth Circuit had failed to give reasons for denied attorney's fees. It was not 1988, it was the Emergency School Aid Act, but they're very closely analogous statutes. The Sixth Circuit had failed to give reasons. That was a 1983 case, wasn't it? If it involved a school, it must have been. It was involved a school. I'm not sure if 1983 or if there may have been other statutory bases, but the statute awarding attorney's fees in that case or providing for the award of attorney's fees is in part. But do you agree that 1988 provides for attorney's fees only in 1983 cases? Yes. Do you agree with that? There are some minor other statutes, yes. You agree with that? And your case involves only 1983? That's correct. Our case involves 1983. But you said it involves several questions. Well, no. There are underlying, I think that the only issue properly before this court is whether the Eighth Circuit should have given a statement of reasons. Well, why? There are, because without a statement of reasons, it is impossible for this court to adequately review what the Eighth Circuit did. Do you know how many cases come from New York where no opinions are written at all and this court decides them? Yes, but at least... The caller, do you know? Quite a few. But at least... Do you think we have to have an opinion in every case in order to decide it? I think that it is important to have an opinion in a case... I didn't say important, I said necessary. That we can't rule without it. Certainly you can rule without it. This court certainly has the power to do so. And don't rule it, repeat. So why do we have to do it in this one? What I am... What makes this one so special? Well, I think what makes it so special in part is that you're dealing with a federal court. And in part, one of the powers that this court has is supervisory powers over the federal courts. This court properly should determine how it wants cases presented to it. What about the Fifth Circuit's rule where they simply affirm by order on the merits, not on costs, without any opinion or any explanation of reasons? You can perhaps justify no opinion where you have a district court opinion below. And the typical abbreviated opinion that I've seen, for the reasons stated below, we affirm. You can, and the Eighth Circuit even has a rule providing for the disposal of frivolous cases that merely says, we reverse or, pardon me, we affirm, and cites the rule. That at least tells the attorney on what basis his case was decided. Here we have no way of determining what the basis was for the decision. Since you have just told us, counsel, that the Eighth Circuit practice recognizes that it's a discretionary power, and sometimes they allow and sometimes they do not allow fees, and you have also said, I think in precisely these words, that it would have satisfied the statute if they had recited. In the exercise of our discretion, the application for fees is denied. Now, doesn't the word deny embrace that just as a denial of cert up here? No, Your Honor, I perhaps... The states, when we deny cert, we don't explain it. We deny, and I think it is accepted that that's in exercise of our discretion. I perhaps put too much emphasis on the words in the exercise of our discretion because I immediately put that in the framework of the statute. The statute, as interpreted, requires an award of attorney's fees unless some very narrow factual circumstances exist. So if the court says in the exercise of our discretion, we deny attorney's fees, that means they've gotten past the legal question of whether or not the statute applies, and as soon as they say we're exercising discretion, you immediately know this must be the reason why they're denied. So in this particular circumstance, exercise of discretion, because the discretion is so narrow as to the award, granted very large as to the amount of the award, but very narrow as to whether or not you do award, it tells you what the court's doing. As a general proposition... I thought I heard you answer my brother Marshall, but if you have no 1983 cause of action, then you have no claim under 1988 for attorney's fees. Is that right? That's correct. In this case, that is correct. May we not then see what you've treated in the way of cause of action, and if we hold there was no 1983 cause of action pleaded, can't we affirm without more? This court certainly can. It has power to do so. Is there any reason we shouldn't? Yes. I think the reason that you shouldn't comes precisely to the point that I was making before. What you should do is establish by what procedure do you want these cases to come before you. If you want circuit courts to decide attorney's fees initially and do so without an opinion, you are going to be continually presented as the only available court of review with petitions for certiorari that are unable to tell you what the issues are. They will be unable to tell you why the lower court decided. They will be unable to tell you what was wrong with the lower court's decision. You will, in effect, be presented again and again with de novo cases, starting out with, we need to prove these things in order to be entitled to attorney's fees, and we think we've proven them all, and go through and the parties can argue about each one of the things that need be proven and every issue under the sun. The point is, if you want to establish a procedure, it is desirable to have the circuit court of appeals state its reasons so that this court can properly exercise its appellate review authority, be able to look at the petition for certiorari, and determine whether this is a case that it should hear or a case that lacks importance to be heard. Do you think 1983 embraces the inverse side of the Commerce Clause? Yes, Your Honor, I do. I perhaps should frame it a little bit more clearly. I think that there is a right to engage in interstate commerce, and I think that that is a fundamental right. I think it was recognized as a fundamental right at the time of the Constitution, and that the Constitution secures that right by putting a provision in it, providing, in effect, at least to some degree, exclusive jurisdiction in Congress to regulate interstate commerce because the drafters recognized that state regulation was inimical to the right to engage in interstate commerce. But Cooley against Board of Wardens, before the Civil War established that Congress's right to regulate interstate commerce was not exclusive. This Court has always held that there are some areas where Congress can regulate, or some sets of circumstances where Congress can regulate but the states cannot. Now, what the definition is of what the states cannot regulate has changed through the 200 years, but there's always been areas where the states can't regulate because they impose an unconstitutional burden, or perhaps because it's direct-indirect regulation depending upon which Commerce Clause test you use. But there's always been held to be an area that is exempt from state regulation, and that's precisely what the drafters intended. The reason the Constitutional Convention was called was because of state regulation of interstate commerce and the destruction of interstate commerce it was causing. That was the original reason. And the answer that the framers gave was to give Congress the power to regulate interstate commerce. That's correct. It did not certainly in height verba say that the states were divested of their authority to regulate interstate commerce, only that if Congress superseded state regulation by congressional action, the state regulation. No. Perhaps as an example, this Court itself in Consolidated Freightways v. Castle, pardon me, Castle v. Consolidated Freightways, the case in chief, held that even though Congress had not acted on the regulation of truck length, there was an area where the state could not act. Well, I said that, and that's why I said the framers in height verba did not say that. That's right. This Court has developed the... That's right. I think the framers certainly intended it, though. There was no great outcry that this Court was broadening the Constitution or unreasonably interpreting it because, as I say, part of the reason for the initial constitutional convention was the recognition that the state regulation was causing problems, and part of the reason for granting the power to Congress was to remove it from the states. You certainly find several instances of this Court referring to the right to engage in interstate commerce free from the wrong kind of state regulation. That's correct. That's correct. The original Gibbons v. Ogden, Justice Marshall, referred to a right to engage in interstate commerce as a natural right of man. This Court, in its Commerce Clause cases, has frequently spoken of a right to be free of improper state regulation. Now, what constitutes improper state regulation, I think, is, you know, in any given case can be debating, but that there is an area where the Constitution, by its own words, removes from the states the power to regulate, whether it be for improper regulation or only certain subject matter or whatever, there is an area that is removed from state regulation. That's the protection, the securing of the right to engage in interstate commerce that we think was violated by Iowa. We had a right, a right to engage in interstate commerce repeatedly recognized by this Court, recognized as a natural and inalienable right. It was secured by the Constitution because one of the purposes of the Commerce Clause was to remove from the state the power to regulate interstate commerce in certain instances, and this was one of those instances, the right was violated. Consequently, 1983 was violated. Mr. Letter, would you agree that if the Court did not agree with that analysis, felt that this really was not a 1983 case and therefore 1988 was not intended to authorize the award of fees in this case, then there would be no duty in the Court of Appeals to give you a statement of reasons? No. If the law is you're not entitled to fees, why do they have to give you a statement of reasons? No. If what you're saying is the Court of Appeals may have decided... That may be the law. Maybe we think Congress did not intend to authorize fees here. Don't you have to persuade us that Congress authorized fees before there would be any duty at all on the Court of Appeals to give a statement of reasons? Well, I think you would at least have to state the reason of you haven't persuaded us. Well, supposing we had a case last year in which we said 1988 doesn't apply to a case like this. Then your fee request was presented to the Court of Appeals. Couldn't they simply deny it without an opinion? I think they could deny it because frivolous. And that's a simple... Would they have to say it's frivolous when it would be obvious that it was? Yes, Your Honor. Well, you just agreed before that if they said denied an exercise of discretion, it would be enough. Denied an exercise of discretion, I think, would be enough because it says in this context... If you get over the first hump that Justice Brennan and Justice Stevens have been talking to you about, the first hump, the 1983 hump. Mm-hmm. Yeah, if it's denied in discretion, then obviously we got over the 1983 hump. No, I'm not suggesting... I'm suggesting the statute said in so many words, no fee shall be allowed in Commerce Clause litigation. Would they still have to give you a statement of reason? No. I think they could do what was their practice and simply say denied Rule 19, which means it's denied because of privilege. They couldn't do what they did here. But yes, they need to give a reason. Supposing you'd ask them not for fees, but supposing you'd ask them for a $400 million judgment on the theory that you don't like your opponent, and they just said denied, would they have to give you a statement of reason? Yes. Let me... You say they have to give me a statement of reason. I'm not so concerned and I'm not resting my case on my need for a statement of reasons. I think the reason that they give... Pardon me? You say we need it. You need it. That's correct. That's precisely correct. And you need it particularly, whereas here, the Eighth Circuit's acting as that initial court, acting as trial court. We need it if we think the law, in effect, says you don't get fees in a case like this. Well, that's perhaps begging the question. Well, it seems to me you've got the burden of convincing us that there's an authorization for fees. Before you can persuade me, at least, there's any reason to give us a statement for denial. If the law doesn't authorize fees, I don't care what reason, whether the Court of Appeals gives you reasons or not. That's right. But the point, perhaps, is if the law doesn't authorize, then no, you don't need to care what reason the Eighth Circuit did, because that's sort of an initial foreclosing question, just as if you concluded that there were no jurisdiction. And I suggest you're the party who's asking for the fees, so it seems to me you have the burden of demonstrating that the statute authorizes fees for you. Well, that may be correct, but you can think of a number of additional factors and additional issues that could foreclose the question. And we very quickly would be back to the original situation of here are ten issues which may have been determinative. We need to argue all ten to persuade you that we should be awarded fees. That may be the case, but it's not a very comfortable way of handling cases. And I suggest one that is going to make this Court's task of review a very difficult task. Do I understand you correctly that if we say the Court has to give you reasons and we send it back saying that, and the Court says our reason is we have exercised our discretion, that's in. Is that your position? Under the peculiar terms of this statute. Is that your position? Yes, sir. Well, what are we doing? Under the peculiar terms. What are we sitting here for? Why don't we just do it that way? Under the peculiar terms of this statute, if you say under the exercise of our discretion, you have immediately told everyone concerned what the reason is. It's because the statute has interpreted in each. You've got to award attorney's fees unless A exists. The reason if a Court just doesn't do something is it's within their discretion not to do it. Isn't that automatic? No, Your Honor. Well, you want the Court to say we don't grant you tax because we don't like it? There are certain statutes that give very limited discretionary powers to the Court. There are certain things that courts must do. 1988 is very close to being one of those statutes because... Well, is it? Pardon me? You say close to, is it? It is not in one circumstance. But if it's not in one... That is, the Court need not award attorney's fees if it finds special circumstances. Special circumstances are very narrowly defined. If the Court says we're not awarding in our discretion, they are saying we found the special circumstance that the statute speaks of. I'd like to reserve the rest of my time. Thank you. Thank you. Mr. Solicitor General. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the Court. Thank you. The Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals held below that Consolidated Freight Waves was not entitled to attorney's fees for the appeal part of the litigation in the case in chief with which this court is previously familiar. Was that, Mr. Schantz, for the appeal part in that court or also here? Only in the... Only in the... Before the Eighth Circuit. And it was... The bill of costs in question was filed before the case came up here. Iowa has consistently taken the position that Dormant Commerce Clause case litigation is not within 1983. We took that position in our answer. We took that position with counsel as the letter to the clerk to which he referred makes clear. We had indicated that we were going to oppose any award of fees. We resisted the bill of costs, indicating that we objected to any award of fees. When they moved to vacate, we made very explicit that in our... It was our contention that 1983 was not applicable. And in our brief, in resistance to the motion to vacate, we developed, admittedly in skeletal form, the contention which is developed in our brief, namely that Commerce Clause cases involve the allocation of governmental power and do not secure individual rights. So we believe that issue was clearly presented to the court below. And we believe... We think it's clearly implicit in the course of the proceeding that that was the basis for the Eighth Circuit's action. But even if it is not, we think it's clear that this court may and would need to address the... may affirm on the ground that we presented below, namely that it was not a 1983 case. This is on the ground that you may defend your judgment in your favor on any ground that you raise below. Exactly. The rule of Langness v. Green and Andridge v. Williams and so on. Congress, the general rule, of course, is that, the American rule, is that fee shifting is not permitted. Congress has authorized fee shifting in certain civil rights statutes under 42 United States Code, Section 1988. The only such statute invoked here is 42 U.S.C. Section 1983. And thus the question becomes whether Section 1983 provides a remedy for dormant Commerce Clause cases. Section 1983 provides a remedy in the language of the statute when there has been a deprivation of a right, privilege, or immunity secured by the Constitution. And the particular question before this Court, then, is whether that language should be construed to reach Commerce Clause cases. Iowa's contention that 1983 does not reach dormant Commerce Clause litigation can usually be divided into two propositions. The first is that the reach of Section 1983 is not coextensive with the Constitution. Not every lawsuit in which a constitutional claim is asserted against a state or a state official involves the deprivation of any rights, privileges, or immunities secured by the Constitution. And the second proposition is that the minor premise, if you will, is that the Commerce Clause should be understood as a provision allocating authority, structuring governmental power, and not as a provision securing rights against government. I think the first proposition, the proposition that the reach of 1983 is not coextensive with the Constitution, must be regarded as well established. In Chapman v. Houston Welfare Rights Organization, this Court held, and with, I believe, without dissent on this point, that litigation against state officials, which invokes the Supremacy Clause, without more, cannot be brought pursuant to 28 U.S.C. Section 1343.3. Now, the language of 1343.3 is completely identical to the language of 1983 as it relates to the Constitution. It certainly didn't say there that because you can't bring it under 1943, you can't bring it under 1331 either. If I understand your question, we would certainly concede that this case can be brought under 1331. Well, in 1983, too. Well, 1983... 1343, just among other things, it removed the amount in controversy. That's correct. But that's all been done away with now anyway. That's correct. In operational consequence, Justice White, I think the only thing at stake here is whether or not attorney's fees are to be awarded in Commerce Clause cases. And if we were to conclude that 1983 doesn't reach it, that would be the end of the case, wouldn't it? Exactly right. Or even if we concluded that 1983 did reach it, it would be the end of the case if we thought that it was presumptively an exercise of discretion, of unexplained denial. This Court certainly could affirm on that ground. You don't want us to reverse if we disagree with you on 1983. Certainly not. Certainly not. General Shantz, let me go back to your reference to Chapman. That held, as I recall, that the jurisdictional statute 1343 is not as broad in its coverage as 1983. That's correct. How is that support for the proposition that 1983 doesn't reach this claim? 1343 speaks in terms of rights secured by the Constitution. That does not include supremacy clause, right? Right. And from then on, 1343, when it refers to laws, refers to civil rights laws. Discuss what this Court held in Houston Welfare Rights. Right. But with respect to the Constitution, rights secured by the Constitution, the language is identical. And in Lynch v. Household Finance, this Court said clearly that with respect to constitutional rights, the reach of 1343, the reach of 1983 are the same. Right. And so if this is, if, but how does that answer the question whether there is a right to engage in interstate commerce, that's a way of phrasing it, or whether 1983 was the cause of action statute in this case? One of the arguments advanced in Chapman was that this was a case involving rights secured by the Constitution. Right. Because it was a case premised on the supremacy clause. Right. A constitutional provision. Correct. And this Court rejected that, I believe, unanimously, saying that, saying that that language, rights secured by the Constitution, doesn't include every Constitution. Did not include the supremacy clause. Rather, that was in the nature of a statutory claim rather than a constitutional claim, based on a violation of the federal statute. But here there's a violation, there's alleged, and I guess we held in the case was here before, that there was a violation of a constitutional provision. We certainly don't mean to contend that Chapman literally controls, because it does not reach the second proposition, but we think it is square authority for the major premise, which is that 1983 is not coextensive with the Constitution.
